posts.reason: Dan Luu's long argument, built on concrete examples of LLM-built software failing in practice, that a developer who just relays what the loop produces is doing a job the company could run without them.
A case against handing colleagues AI-written design docs, PRs and summaries, paired with the author's own line between what he let the model do on a paper and what he wrote himself.

Argues that a postmortem should end with what will change, not with a good explanation, because a satisfying 'why' can kill the urgency to fix anything; the thread pushes back on leaders who skip the specifics.
Names a common failure after promotion to senior (overreach, silence, hidden overwork, burnout) and a way out: become the most helpful person on the team and rebuild trust with steady, visible work.
A careful, footnoted essay on why most organs barely heal while the liver regrows, built on one idea (regeneration buys cancer risk), and a thread where a pathologist and others dig into vitamin A.
Shows the arithmetic behind a large saving: derived error formulas that justified cutting hash points per server by 90%, and a rollout staged per data center to avoid a global cache flush.
A short question that draws concrete interview formats from people who run them: debugging a deliberately broken codebase, pairing without AI, agentic take-homes.
Concrete before-and-after timings for each CI change in a large TypeScript monorepo: native TypeScript compiler, lint without type information, leaner installs, Vitest sharding.
A workable method for treating an LLM as a copyeditor rather than a ghostwriter, with two strict rules, and a thread of developers applying it to commit messages and PR descriptions.
An open-source desktop tool where coding agents draw sequence, ER and architecture diagrams linked to code, with a decision log, and a thread comparing it with C4 and PlantUML.
A long, illustrated essay arguing that classic pixel art owed its look more to dithering, anti-aliasing and palette choices than to CRT blur, with C64, Amiga, SNES and VGA examples.
